lead: A pushdown automaton (PDA) is a finite automaton with a stack. The stack has no size limit, so the machine can remember a count or nesting depth and match it later. That extra store describes every context-free language. PDAs appear in compiler front ends, JSON and XML validators, and bracket checkers. This chapter gives the formal definition and the notation for one run, one move at a time.
prereq: You need DFA and NFA definitions, transition tables and the extended transition function from Unit 1 (Deterministic finite automata and Nondeterministic finite automata).

blocks.text: A PDA is a finite automaton plus one stack. The finite control is still states and a move table, as in a DFA (Unit 1, Deterministic finite automata). The stack gives memory that grows and shrinks with input.
P = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z₀, F)
blocks.where: Q is a finite set of states; Σ is the input alphabet; Γ is the stack alphabet; δ is the transition function; q₀ ∈ Q is the start state; Z₀ ∈ Γ is the initial stack symbol; F ⊆ Q is the set of final states.

blocks.text: The stack appears in δ. Here 2^(Q × Γ*) means the set of all subsets of Q × Γ*.

blocks.where: one call δ(q, a, X) takes a state q, one input symbol a (or ε for no input), and top stack symbol X, and returns a set of pairs. Each pair (p, β) means: go to state p and replace X by β ∈ Γ*.

blocks.text: Read (q, a, X) → (p, γ) as: in q, reading a with X on top, go to p and replace X by γ. The leftmost symbol of γ becomes the new top. Three cases cover everything:

items: γ = ε: pop X; the stack shrinks by one.
γ = X: the stack is unchanged.
γ = YX: push Y above X; X remains below.

blocks.text: When a = ε the move reads nothing and the input pointer stays put. Books call the stack alphabet Γ, Z or Π; the stack is also the pushdown store or pushdown list. These are the same object.

sections.h3: Instantaneous descriptions and the move relation

blocks.text: At any moment three things capture the machine: current state, unread input, and whole stack. This triple is the instantaneous description (ID), written (q, w, γ).
Here q ∈ Q is state; w ∈ Σ* is unread input (read symbols are gone); γ ∈ Γ* is full stack with top at left. For stack AAZ₀, top is A and bottom is Z₀. The start ID for input w is (q₀, w, Z₀).
(q, aw, Xγ) ⊢ (p, w, βγ) when (p, β) ∈ δ(q, a, X)
blocks.where: q and p are states; a is one input symbol or ε; w is the unread input after that symbol; X is the top stack symbol; γ is the rest of the stack below X; β is the string pushed in place of X. The relation ⊢ is one move.

blocks.text: ⊢* is the reflexive-transitive closure of ⊢: x ⊢* y means y is reached from x in zero or more moves. Writing IDs with ⊢ between them gives the trace.

In a diagram, an arrow q → p labelled a, X / γ means read a, pop X, push γ. Two arrows for the same (q, a, X) make the machine nondeterministic: δ returns more than one pair (contrast in 4.3). Acceptance conventions are in 4.2.
Examples use P = ({q₀, q₁, q₂}, {a, b}, {Z₀, A}, δ, q₀, Z₀, {q₂}). Only five entries of δ are non-empty; every other triple returns ∅, so no move is possible.

First two rows push one A per a. Next two pop one A per b; the first pop also enters q₁. Last row moves on ε without reading input. Z₀ is a bottom marker, so the machine never pops an empty stack: b moves stop when Z₀ is exposed. The machine counts a's, then matches b's, and accepts {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}.

examples.question: For P above, (a) trace IDs for aabb, one move per line. (b) Give move count and final stack height. (c) Give L(P).
steps: Read a, top Z₀: δ(q₀, a, Z₀) = {(q₀, AZ₀)} gives (q₀, abb, AZ₀).
Read a, top A: δ(q₀, a, A) = {(q₀, AA)} gives (q₀, bb, AAZ₀); two A's sit over Z₀.
Read b, top A: δ(q₀, b, A) = {(q₁, ε)} gives (q₁, b, AZ₀).
Read b, top A: δ(q₁, b, A) = {(q₁, ε)} gives (q₁, ε, Z₀).
No input, top Z₀: δ(q₁, ε, Z₀) = {(q₂, Z₀)} gives (q₂, ε, Z₀).
Run length 4 input symbols; moves = 2 pushes + 2 pops + 1 ε-move = 5; final stack height 1 (Z₀). q₂ ∈ F, so aabb is accepted. Same pattern accepts exactly {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}.
examples.answer: Trace: (q₀, aabb, Z₀) ⊢ (q₀, abb, AZ₀) ⊢ (q₀, bb, AAZ₀) ⊢ (q₁, b, AZ₀) ⊢ (q₁, ε, Z₀) ⊢ (q₂, ε, Z₀). The run takes 5 moves, 1 symbol remains on the stack, and L(P) = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}.
examples.check:
w = "aabb"
n = len(w)
na = w.count("a")
nb = w.count("b")
moves = 2 * na + 1   # one push per a, one pop per b, one epsilon move
stack_end = 1        # only Z0 remains
print(n)
print(na)
print(nb)
print(moves)
print(stack_end)

traps: Top is left. Pushing A on Z₀ gives AZ₀, never Z₀A. The leftmost symbol of γ is top in every ID and push.
δ returns a set. An entry can have zero, one or several pairs; several at the same (q, a, X) means nondeterminism.
Do not reverse γ. If γ = YX, Y is top and X stays below; reversing γ accepts wrong strings.
ε-move consumes no input. In (q₁, ε, Z₀) ⊢ (q₂, ε, Z₀), remaining input is ε on both sides.
Z₀ need not be popped. The bottom marker normally stays; acceptance conventions are in 4.2.

quiz.q: List the seven components of a pushdown automaton and say what each one is.
quiz.a: P = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z₀, F): Q states, Σ input alphabet, Γ stack alphabet, δ transition function, q₀ start state, Z₀ initial stack symbol, F final states.

quiz.q: In the ID (q, w, γ), which parts are input and which are stack, and where is the top of the stack?
quiz.a: q is the current state, w ∈ Σ* is the unread input, γ ∈ Γ* is the whole stack with its top at the left end.

quiz.q: Why is an entry of δ allowed to contain more than one pair?
quiz.a: Because the PDA may be nondeterministic. δ(q, a, X) is a set; several pairs mean several legal moves from the same state, input symbol and top symbol, and the machine may take any of them.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between the moves γ = ε, γ = X and γ = YX in a transition.
quiz.a: γ = ε pops X, so the stack shrinks by one. γ = X leaves the stack unchanged. γ = YX pushes Y above X, so the stack grows and the old X is still below.

quiz.q: For the worked machine, give the ID after the two a's of aabb have been read, and give the move count for the input aaabbb.
quiz.a: After two a's, the ID is (q₀, bb, AAZ₀). For aaabbb: 3 pushes + 3 pops + 1 ε-move = 7 moves, and the stack ends with just Z₀.

quiz.q: Using the same machine, show the full trace for the input ab and say how many moves the run takes.
quiz.a: (q₀, ab, Z₀) ⊢ (q₀, b, AZ₀) ⊢ (q₁, ε, Z₀) ⊢ (q₂, ε, Z₀). The run takes 3 moves, and ab is accepted.

quiz.q: Suppose δ(q₁, b, A) were changed to {(q₁, AA)} instead of {(q₁, ε)}. What happens on input aabb, and why?
quiz.a: Trace: (q₀, aabb, Z₀) ⊢ (q₀, abb, AZ₀) ⊢ (q₀, bb, AAZ₀) ⊢ (q₁, b, AZ₀) ⊢ (q₁, ε, AAZ₀). State q₁, stack AAZ₀, top A, no input left; the ε-move on Z₀ cannot fire, so aabb is rejected. The machine now pushes on a and on b alike and never balances them.

quiz.q: If you delete every stack operation from a PDA, keeping only states and input, what kind of machine is left, and what does that tell you?
quiz.a: What is left is an NFA over Σ, because each move now only chooses a next state on a symbol or on ε. So a PDA is an NFA whose moves also depend on the top symbol and which also writes a string. The stack is the only extra power, and it lifts the machine from regular languages to context-free languages (see 4.4).

beyond: Not for the exam. Parser generators build δ for real parsers and keep the unexpanded derivation on the stack. Java bytecode runs on a stack machine, and verifiers check stack discipline like a PDA checks brackets. Research uses pushdown systems for recursive-program bug finding and visibly pushdown automata for fast verification.
